name: Lutein
short: Cohort, 77,126 aged 50-76: over 4 years of individual lutein supplements linked to doubled lung cancer risk (association). AREDS2, 50-85, macular disease risk: lutein/zeaxanthin rise not significant.
text: The main safety data come from the AREDS2 trial in 4203 people aged 50 to 85 at risk of advanced macular degeneration, who were randomised to lutein plus zeaxanthin, omega-3 fatty acids (DHA plus EPA), both, or placebo; all were also asked to take the original AREDS formula (vitamins C and E, beta carotene and zinc) or to accept randomisation to a variation of it. In the trial, more lung cancers occurred in the beta carotene group than in the no beta carotene group, mostly in former smokers, and the investigators suggested lutein plus zeaxanthin as a substitute carotenoid. In a 10-year follow-up of 3882 participants, the odds of lung cancer were 1.82 (95% CI 1.06 to 3.12) for those assigned beta carotene and 1.15 (95% CI 0.79 to 1.66), not statistically significant, for those assigned lutein/zeaxanthin. In an observational cohort of 77,126 adults aged 50 to 76 in Washington State, who reported their use of multivitamins and individual supplements or mixtures over the previous 10 years, longer use of individual lutein supplements was associated with a statistically significantly higher risk of lung cancer (hazard ratio 2.02, 95% CI 1.28 to 3.17, for more than 4 years of use versus no use); the link was with duration of use, not with total 10-year average dose, the authors found little evidence that it differed by sex or smoking status, and the abstract does not say what the individual supplements contained besides lutein; this is an association, not proof of cause. In a randomised dose-ranging trial in 45 people aged 60 or older with or without age-related macular degeneration, given one of three doses of lutein by mouth for 6 months (the abstract describes no placebo group), no toxicity was observed with any dose, and the authors said a long-term large trial is needed to investigate the safety and efficacy of lutein. A Cochrane review found that lutein/zeaxanthin may have little or no effect on mortality (very low-certainty evidence) and noted that most studies were too small to detect rare adverse effects. A review describes lutein as Generally Regarded as Safe with minimal side effects on long-term consumption. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
